title: Acute Liver Failure

AASLD guidance recommends the King's College Criteria for transplant-listing decisions in acute liver failure.
Exact criteria thresholds WebSearch-verified against multiple contemporary sources before writing.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-14, Batch 4).

summary: Acute liver failure is coagulopathy plus encephalopathy in a patient with no prior liver disease and a short illness course — the King's College Criteria (different thresholds for acetaminophen vs. other causes) drive transplant-center referral timing, and a few genuine counterintuitive management points (NAC beyond acetaminophen, not correcting coagulopathy prophylactically) matter.
whyThisMatters: Acute liver failure can deteriorate from 'sick but talking' to cerebral edema and herniation within hours to days, and the decision to transfer to a transplant center needs to happen BEFORE that deterioration — not after, when transport itself becomes dangerous — so recognizing King's-College-positive criteria early, and referring on that basis rather than waiting for the patient to look sicker, is the actionable point.
clinicalTakeaway: Any patient with new coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5) AND any degree of encephalopathy, with no prior liver disease and illness onset within the past 26 weeks, has acute liver failure until proven otherwise — call your transplant center early. For acetaminophen-induced ALF, arterial pH < 7.3 (after adequate fluid resuscitation) ALONE is sufficient to trigger transplant-center referral, without needing to wait for the full triad. Give N-acetylcysteine regardless of etiology — it has a mortality benefit even in non-acetaminophen ALF, not just the classic overdose indication.

body.text: Acute liver failure = new-onset coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5) PLUS any degree of hepatic encephalopathy, in a patient with NO pre-existing liver disease and an illness duration of less than 26 weeks. The distinction from decompensated CHRONIC liver disease (cirrhosis) matters — this reference is about the acute, previously-healthy-liver presentation.
King's College Criteria — when to call the transplant center

Two separate criteria sets, because acetaminophen-induced and non-acetaminophen-induced ALF behave differently prognostically. Meeting criteria means the patient has a poor predicted survival WITHOUT transplant and should prompt urgent transplant-center referral — it doesn't mean transplant is certain or immediate, but the conversation needs to start now, not later.

rows:
Arterial pH < 7.3 (after adequate fluid resuscitation) ALONE — sufficient by itself. 
 OR the triad: INR > 6.5 (PT > 100s) AND creatinine > 3.4 mg/dL AND grade III-IV hepatic encephalopathy.

INR > 6.5 ALONE, regardless of encephalopathy grade. 
 OR any 3 of these 5: age < 10 or > 40 years; etiology is indeterminate or drug-induced (non-acetaminophen); jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval > 7 days; INR > 3.5; bilirubin > 17.4 mg/dL (300 µmol/L).

body.text: The pH < 7.3 acetaminophen criterion, and the INR > 6.5 non-acetaminophen criterion, are each SINGLE criteria sufficient on their own — you don't need the rest of the triad/5-factor list if either of those specific numbers is met.
Management — including a few counterintuitive points

items: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) for ALL acute liver failure, not just acetaminophen-induced — evidence supports a mortality/transplant-free-survival benefit even in non-acetaminophen ALF, likely via improved hepatic microcirculation and antioxidant effect, not just as a specific antidote.

Do NOT prophylactically correct the coagulopathy (FFP, vitamin K) in the absence of active bleeding or before an invasive procedure — the elevated INR is a PROGNOSTIC MARKER the team needs to track, and correcting it masks the trend that's actually informing transplant urgency and clinical trajectory. Reserve correction for active bleeding or immediately before a genuinely necessary invasive procedure.

Monitor closely for cerebral edema as encephalopathy grade rises (grade III-IV in particular) — this is the feared, potentially fatal complication. Head-of-bed elevation, avoiding hypotonic fluids, and treating triggers (agitation, seizures, hypercapnia) are first-line; hypertonic saline or mannitol and ICP monitoring are next-level interventions per neurocritical care/transplant-center guidance once cerebral edema is a real concern.
Correct hypoglycemia aggressively and check it frequently — impaired gluconeogenesis makes ALF patients prone to it, and it can itself worsen encephalopathy/mimic its progression.

Treat/prevent infection proactively — ALF patients are functionally immunocompromised and infection is a major driver of deterioration and a contraindication to transplant if uncontrolled at the time of listing.
Avoid sedation where possible, or use short-acting agents titrated carefully — sedation can mask a genuine decline in mental status that the team needs to be tracking.
